lessons.title: Sugarcane Varieties and Selection Criteria
lessons.body: Choosing the right sugarcane variety is the first step to a profitable harvest. In Africa, common varieties include NCo376 (high sucrose, good for irrigated areas), CP72-1312 (drought-tolerant, suited to drylands), and R570 (resistant to smut, widely grown in South Africa). Local agricultural research stations, like the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) or the Sugarcane Research Institute in Tanzania, can advise on varieties best for your region. Key selection criteria are: maturity period (early, mid, or late), sucrose content (measured as pol% cane, ideally above 12%), resistance to pests and diseases (especially smut, rust, and mosaic), and tolerance to drought or waterlogging. For rain-fed areas, choose early-maturing varieties like Co421 that can be harvested in 12 months. For irrigated farms, late-maturing high-yield varieties like N14 can be grown for 18 months. Always buy certified seed cane from reputable sources to avoid disease. Inspect seed cane for signs of pests like scale insects or borers. Plant at least two or three different varieties to spread risk. For example, if you plant only one variety and it succumbs to rust, you lose everything. A good practice is to allocate 70% of your land to a proven high-yielder and 30% to a new variety you want to test. Remember, variety choice affects everything from planting density to harvest timing. Consult your local extension officer before planting.

lessons.title: Soil Preparation and Planting Techniques
lessons.body: Sugarcane grows best in deep, well-drained loamy soils with a pH between 6.0 and 7.5. Start by clearing the land of bushes and previous crop residues. Plough to a depth of 30-40 cm, then harrow to break clods. If the soil is acidic (pH below 5.5), apply agricultural lime at 2-4 tonnes per hectare and incorporate it into the top 15 cm. For planting, use the furrow method: dig furrows 20-30 cm deep and 90-120 cm apart. In dry areas, make furrows 15 cm deep and space them 1.5 m apart to conserve moisture. Place seed cane (setts) in the furrows, overlapping them slightly. Each sett should have 2-3 buds. A common spacing is 3-4 setts per meter of furrow. Cover with 5-8 cm of soil. Planting time depends on rainfall: in East Africa, plant with the long rains (March-May) or short rains (October-December). In West Africa, plant at the onset of the rainy season. Apply a starter fertilizer at planting: 200 kg/ha of DAP (18-46-0) or 150 kg/ha of TSP. For organic options, use well-rotted manure at 10-15 tonnes per hectare. After planting, apply a pre-emergence herbicide like atrazine to control weeds. If you plant on slopes, use contour furrows to prevent erosion. For smallholder farmers, hand planting with a hoe is common, but for larger fields, tractor-drawn planters save time. Ensure the soil is moist at planting; if dry, irrigate lightly. Germination occurs in 2-4 weeks. Gap-fill after 4 weeks to maintain plant population.

lessons.title: Irrigation and Fertilization Practices
lessons.body: Sugarcane is a thirsty crop, needing 1500-2500 mm of water per year. In dry areas, irrigation is essential. The most common methods in Africa are furrow irrigation (flooding the furrows), sprinkler, and drip. Furrow irrigation is cheap but uses a lot of water; drip irrigation saves up to 50% water but has high initial cost. Irrigate every 7-10 days in sandy soils and every 14 days in clay soils. Critical stages for water are tillering (2-4 months) and grand growth (4-10 months). Stop irrigation 30 days before harvest to increase sucrose. For fertilization, conduct a soil test first. A typical recommendation for a 12-month crop is 120 kg N, 60 kg P2O5, and 120 kg K2O per hectare. Split nitrogen: apply half at planting and half at 6-8 weeks after planting. Use urea (46% N) or ammonium sulphate. Phosphorus is applied at planting as DAP or TSP. Potassium as muriate of potash (MOP) at planting. In sandy soils, apply 30 kg/ha of magnesium sulphate if deficiency symptoms (yellowing between veins) appear. Organic farmers can use poultry manure (5-10 t/ha) or compost. Foliar sprays of micronutrients like zinc and boron can correct deficiencies. Over-fertilizing with nitrogen causes lodging (falling over) and reduces sugar content. Always apply fertilizer when soil is moist and cover lightly. Keep records of all applications for future planning.

lessons.title: Pest and Disease Management in Sugarcane
lessons.body: The most destructive sugarcane pests in Africa are the spotted stem borer (Chilo sacchariphagus), the African sugarcane borer (Eldana saccharina), and termites. Borers tunnel into stalks, reducing sugar yield and causing dead hearts. Monitor with pheromone traps or by scouting for shot-hole damage on leaves. For control, release biological agents like Cotesia flavipes (a parasitic wasp) or apply insecticides such as carbofuran at planting. Termites attack setts and roots; treat setts with imidacloprid before planting. Diseases include smut (caused by Sporisorium scitamineum), ratoon stunting disease (RSD), and mosaic virus. Smut shows as black whip-like structures on the growing point. Uproot and burn infected plants. RSD causes stunted growth and is spread through infected seed cane; use disease-free seed and sterilize cutting tools with 10% bleach. Mosaic virus causes yellow-green mottling; control aphids that spread it. For all diseases, plant resistant varieties. Practice crop rotation with legumes like beans or groundnuts to break pest cycles. Keep fields weed-free because weeds host pests. Avoid over-irrigation, which promotes fungal diseases. Regular field scouting is key: walk your fields weekly and look for unusual symptoms. If you see more than 5% of plants affected, take action. Consult your extension officer for approved pesticides and follow safety instructions. Always wear protective clothing when spraying.

lessons.title: Harvesting Methods: Manual vs. Mechanical
lessons.body: Harvesting sugarcane at the right time is crucial for maximum sugar recovery. The crop is ready when it is 12-18 months old, depending on variety, and when a sample of stalks shows a Brix reading of 18-22% using a hand refractometer. Harvesting too early gives low sugar; too late gives fibrous, low-juice cane. Manual harvesting is common in Africa: workers use machetes or cane knives to cut stalks at ground level, then remove leaves and tops. A skilled worker can cut 1-2 tonnes per day. Manual harvesting is labor-intensive but gives cleaner cane and is suitable for small fields and uneven terrain. Mechanical harvesting uses combine harvesters that cut, chop, and load cane into trailers. These machines can harvest 200-400 tonnes per day but are expensive and require large, flat fields. They also leave more trash in the cane, which can reduce sugar recovery. In Africa, mechanical harvesters are used on large estates in South Africa, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. For most smallholders, manual harvesting is the only option. After cutting, leave the cane in windrows for a day to dry slightly, then load onto trucks. Avoid burning before harvest unless necessary; burning removes leaves but can damage cane if too hot. If you burn, do it 2-3 hours before cutting and ensure the fire does not spread. Harvest during the dry season when sugar content is highest. Cut stalks close to the ground (within 2 cm) to maximize yield. After harvest, ratoon the crop for 2-3 more cycles before replanting.

lessons.title: Post-Harvest Handling and Transport to Mill
lessons.body: After cutting, sugarcane starts losing sugar immediately. The sucrose content drops by about 0.5% per day if left in the field. Therefore, transport to the mill should happen within 24-48 hours. First, load cane onto trucks or tractor-drawn trailers. For manual loading, use pitchforks or hands; for mechanical, use grab loaders. Stack cane loosely to allow air circulation and prevent heating. Do not overload trucks; keep loads within legal weight limits. If the mill is far (over 50 km), cover the load with a tarpaulin to reduce moisture loss. In hot weather, sprinkle water on the cane to keep it cool. At the mill, cane is weighed and tested for sucrose (pol% cane). Payment is based on weight and quality. To maintain quality, avoid mixing old and fresh cane. If you must store cane temporarily, keep it in a shaded area and do not pile it more than 1.5 m high. For smallholder cooperatives, schedule harvesting so that trucks arrive at the mill just in time. Delays cause sugar loss and lower income. Also, clean the cane: remove excess trash, roots, and soil. Mud on cane adds weight but reduces sugar content and can damage mill equipment. After delivery, the mill may return molasses or bagasse as by-products; use them for animal feed or compost. Keep records of each load: weight, date, and quality. This helps you track performance and plan better.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sugarcane Agriculture and Harvesting

This practical reference is written for African agribusiness operators, outgrower scheme managers, estate farm supervisors, and mill procurement teams who need field-level decisions that protect cane supply, sugar recovery, and margin. In most African sugarcane systems â from Kenya's Nyando and Mumias belts, Tanzania's Kilombero and Mtibwa estates, Uganda's Busoga region, South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal Midlands, Eswatini's Lowveld, Malawi's Dwangwa and Nchalo schemes, to Nigeria's Bacita and Savannah Sugar estates â profitability is decided long before the cane reaches the mill gate. Variety choice, planting date, irrigation discipline, pest control, harvest scheduling, and haulage logistics determine sucrose content, fibre levels, and the tonnage that actually gets paid for. A 1% loss in recoverable sucrose across a 100,000-tonne crop is roughly 1,000 tonnes of sugar lost; at prevailing regional prices, that is a material revenue gap. This module gives you the practical benchmarks, tables, and checklists to reduce that gap.

1. Variety Selection and Matching to Agro-Ecology

Variety choice is the single highest-leverage decision in sugarcane agriculture because it locks in yield potential, ratooning ability, disease resistance, and maturity window for 5â8 years. In Africa, the dominant commercial varieties include NCo376 (widely grown in South Africa, Eswatini, and Zimbabwe), N14 and N25 in South Africa, Co421 and Co617 in East Africa, and locally bred selections from the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO), the South African Sugarcane Research Institute (SASRI), and the Tanzania Sugarcane Research Institute (TSRI). Selection must match rainfall, altitude, soil type, harvest season, and mill payment formula (which may reward sucrose content, fibre, or both).

Key selection criteria:

  • Sucrose content (Pol % cane): Target 12â14% for commercial estates; below 10% erodes mill economics.
  • Maturity window: Early, mid, and late maturing varieties spread harvest load and extend the milling season.
  • Ratooning ability: Good ratoons reduce replanting cost, which can be 20â30% of total production cost per cycle.
  • Disease resistance: Especially against smut, mosaic, rust, and ratoon stunting disease (RSD).
  • Drought and waterlogging tolerance: Critical in rain-fed African systems with erratic rainfall.
  • Fibre content: Higher fibre aids mechanical harvesting but reduces mill throughput.

2. Soil Preparation and Planting Techniques

Sugarcane is a heavy feeder with a deep root system. In African conditions, soil preparation determines how well the crop survives dry spells and how efficiently it uses fertiliser. On estates in Malawi and Zambia, deep ripping to 40â50 cm followed by harrowing is standard; on smallholder plots in Kenya and Uganda, minimum tillage with furrow opening at 20â25 cm is more realistic. Planting material should be 8â10 month old, disease-free, and treated against RSD and smut.

Recommended planting parameters:

  • Row spacing: 1.2â1.5 m for commercial estates; 0.9â1.2 m for smallholders to improve weed competition.
  • Seed rate: 8â10 tonnes of cane per hectare for three-bud setts; 6â8 t/ha for two-bud setts.
  • Planting depth: 10â15 cm, covered with 5 cm of soil.
  • Planting window: Align with onset of rains; late planting reduces yield by 15â30% in rain-fed systems.
  • Soil pH: 5.5â7.0; lime if below 5.0.
Table 1: Indicative Sugarcane Yield and Cost Benchmarks in Selected African Systems
Country / System Typical Yield (t/ha) Production Cost (USD/t cane) Dominant Variety Source

Tanzania (Kilombero, estate) 80â110 22â30 NCo376, Co945 TSRI / FAO, 2019
South Africa (KZN Midlands) 75â95 25â35 N14, N25, NCo376 SASRI, 2021
Uganda (Busoga, outgrower) 50â70 30â40 Co421, NCo376 Uganda Sugar Manufacturers' Association, 2020
Malawi (Dwangwa, estate) 90â120 20â28 N14, NCo376 Illovo / FAO, 2019

3. Irrigation and Fertilisation Practices

Sugarcane requires 1,200â1,800 mm of water per cycle. In rain-fed African systems, supplementary irrigation during the grand growth phase (3â9 months) can raise yields by 20â40%. Drip and furrow irrigation are common on estates; smallholders rely on rain and occasional flood irrigation. Fertiliser should be split: basal at planting (P and K), and top-dressings of nitrogen at 6â8 weeks and 12â14 weeks. Over-application of nitrogen late in the season lowers sucrose content.

Indicative fertiliser programme per hectare:

  • Nitrogen (N): 120â180 kg/ha, split into two or three applications.
  • Phosphorus (PâOâ): 60â100 kg/ha at planting.
  • Potassium (KâO): 80â120 kg/ha at planting.
  • Organic matter: Return trash and filter cake to fields to improve soil health and reduce fertiliser dependence.
Table 2: Sugarcane Water and Nutrient Requirements by Growth Stage
Growth Stage Duration (months) Water Requirement (mm) Key Nutrients Management Priority
Germination & establishment 0â2 150â250 P, K, N (basal) Moisture at planting, weed control
Tillering 2â4 200â300 N (first top-dress) Weed competition, pest scouting
Grand growth 4â9 500â700 N, K (second top-dress) Irrigation scheduling, pest control
Maturation / ripening 9â12+ 250â400 Reduced N, K Withhold irrigation, monitor sucrose

Source: FAO, Good Practices for the Production of Sugarcane (2019); SASRI, Fertiliser and Irrigation Guidelines (2021).

4. Pest and Disease Management

The major African sugarcane pests include the stalk borer (Eldana saccharina, Chilo partellus), termites, white grubs, and the sugarcane aphid. Major diseases include smut, mosaic, rust, ratoon stunting disease (RSD), and yellow leaf syndrome. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is the standard: resistant varieties, clean seed, crop rotation, biological control (e.g., Cotesia flavipes for borers), and targeted chemical use only when thresholds are exceeded.

Practical measures:

  • Use certified disease-free seed cane and hot-water treat setts against RSD.
  • Scout weekly during tillering and grand growth; record borer damage in 10 random stools per 5 ha.
  • Release biological control agents where established (e.g., Cotesia flavipes in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda).
  • Rogue out smut-infected stools and burn them away from the field.
  • Rotate with legumes or maize where possible to break pest cycles.

â  SAFETY WARNING â HARVESTING AND BURNING

Burning cane before manual harvest is still practiced in parts of Africa to remove leaf trash and reduce harvest labour. This creates serious risks: flash fires, burns, smoke inhalation, and heat stress. Always:

  • Notify neighbouring farms, the mill, and local authorities before burning.
  • Establish firebreaks of at least 6 m and keep water bowsers on standby.
  • Never burn in high wind or extreme heat; harvest within 24â48 hours of burning to avoid sucrose loss and deterioration.
  • Provide cutters with long-sleeved clothing, boots, gloves, eye protection, and drinking water.
  • Mechanical harvesters must have roll-over protection, fire extinguishers, and trained operators.
  • Respect local by-laws and mill policies on burning; many mills now penalise burnt cane due to lower sugar recovery.

5. Harvesting Methods: Manual vs. Mechanical

Manual harvesting remains dominant in most African outgrower systems because it is labour-intensive but capital-light. Mechanical harvesting is increasingly used on large estates in South Africa, Eswatini, Malawi, and Zambia, where labour costs are rising and fields are flat and well-prepared. The choice affects cane quality, soil compaction, and the mill's ability to process cane quickly.

Manual harvesting: Cutters remove tops, trash, and roots; cane is stacked or loaded by hand. Advantages: lower capital cost, selective cutting, less soil compaction. Disadvantages: slow, labour-dependent, higher trash content, and risk of delays that reduce sucrose.

Mechanical harvesting: Chopper harvesters cut, chop, and load cane into infield wagons or trucks. Advantages: high throughput (up to 400 t/day), reduced labour, faster delivery to mill. Disadvantages: high capital and maintenance cost, soil compaction, higher extraneous matter, and need for field layout and haulage coordination.

Decision rule: if labour availability is unreliable, fields are flat and larger than 200 ha, and the mill can accept chopped cane, mechanical harvesting is usually more cost-effective. If fields are small, steep, or fragmented, manual harvesting with improved logistics is often better.

6. Post-Harvest Handling and Transport to Mill

Sucrose begins to degrade immediately after cutting. In hot African conditions, cane should reach the mill within 24â48 hours; every 24-hour delay can reduce recoverable sucrose by 0.5â1.5%. Key practices:

  • Cut cane close to the ground (5â10 cm) to maximise recoverable stalk.
  • Remove tops and trash to reduce extraneous matter; burnt cane must be processed within 24 hours.
  • Load cane within 6 hours of cutting; avoid leaving cane in the field overnight.
  • Use covered or shaded transport where possible to reduce moisture loss and heat damage.
  • Coordinate with mill scheduling to avoid long queues at the weighbridge.
  • Keep haulage records: tonnes, field, variety, harvest date, and delivery time. This data is essential for payment disputes and yield analysis.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Select varieties matched to rainfall, soil, harvest window, and mill payment formula; confirm disease resistance.
  2. Prepare soil to 40â50 cm depth where possible; plant certified, treated seed cane at 8â10 t/ha.
  3. Apply basal P and K at planting; split N top-dressings at 6â8 and 12â14 weeks.
  4. Irrigate to supplement rainfall during grand growth; withhold water 4â6 weeks before harvest.
  5. Scout weekly for borers, aphids, and smut; use IPM and biological control before chemicals.
  6. If burning, establish firebreaks, notify authorities, and harvest within 24â48 hours.
  7. Cut close to ground, remove tops and trash, and deliver cane to mill within 24â48 hours.
  8. Record every load: field, variety, tonnes, harvest time, and delivery time for payment and yield tracking.

quiz.q: Which sugarcane variety is known for high sucrose and is suitable for irrigated areas?
quiz.explanation: NCo376 is a high-sucrose variety recommended for irrigated conditions.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH range for sugarcane?
quiz.explanation: Sugarcane grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soils with pH 6.0-7.5.

quiz.q: How deep should furrows be for planting sugarcane in dry areas?
quiz.explanation: In dry areas, shallower furrows (15 cm) help conserve moisture.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is commonly applied at planting for sugarcane?
quiz.explanation: DAP (18-46-0) is a common starter fertilizer applied at planting.

quiz.q: What is the critical water requirement stage for sugarcane?
quiz.explanation: Tillering and grand growth stages are most critical for water.

quiz.q: Which pest is a major sugarcane borer in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Stem borers like Eldana saccharina are destructive pests in Africa.

quiz.q: What is a symptom of sugarcane smut?
quiz.explanation: Smut causes black whip-like structures on the growing point.

quiz.q: How can you control ratoon stunting disease?
quiz.explanation: RSD is spread through infected seed cane, so use clean planting material.

quiz.q: What is the ideal Brix reading for harvesting sugarcane?
quiz.explanation: Brix of 18-22% indicates optimal sugar content for harvest.

quiz.q: How many tonnes per day can a skilled manual harvester cut?
quiz.explanation: A skilled worker can manually harvest 1-2 tonnes per day.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of mechanical harvesting?
quiz.explanation: Mechanical harvesters are expensive to purchase and maintain.

quiz.q: How soon should sugarcane be transported to the mill after cutting?
quiz.explanation: Sucrose loss starts immediately, so transport within 24-48 hours is ideal.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mud on harvested cane?
quiz.explanation: Mud reduces sugar content and can damage mill equipment.

quiz.q: What is a common biological control agent for sugarcane borers?
quiz.explanation: Cotesia flavipes is a parasitic wasp used against stem borers.

quiz.q: Which macronutrient is split-applied for sugarcane?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen is applied in split doses to match crop uptake.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing between furrows in dry areas?
quiz.explanation: Wider spacing (1.5 m) helps conserve moisture in dry areas.

quiz.q: Which disease causes yellow-green mottling on leaves?
quiz.explanation: Mosaic virus causes mottling and is spread by aphids.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of applying lime to sugarcane soil?
quiz.explanation: Lime raises soil pH if it is too acidic.

quiz.q: How many ratoon crops can be taken before replanting?
quiz.explanation: Typically 2-3 ratoon cycles are economical before replanting.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of drip irrigation for sugarcane?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation can save up to 50% water compared to furrow.

quiz.q: Which tool is used for manual harvesting?
quiz.explanation: Machetes or cane knives are standard for manual harvesting.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see more than 5% of plants with pest damage?
quiz.explanation: A 5% threshold triggers control measures to prevent spread.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth for ploughing sugarcane fields?
quiz.explanation: Deep ploughing to 30-40 cm breaks hardpan and improves root growth.

quiz.q: Which by-product can be returned from the mill for use as animal feed?
quiz.explanation: Molasses, bagasse, and filter mud are all useful by-products.

quiz.q: What is the first step in soil preparation for sugarcane?
quiz.explanation: Clearing bushes and residues is the first step before ploughing.

quiz.q: How many buds should a good seed sett have?
quiz.explanation: Setts with 2-3 buds ensure good germination.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of manual harvesting?
quiz.explanation: Manual harvesting delivers cleaner cane with less trash.

quiz.q: Which insect spreads mosaic virus?
quiz.explanation: Aphids are the primary vectors of sugarcane mosaic virus.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of farmyard manure for sugarcane?
quiz.explanation: Well-rotted manure at 10-15 t/ha is a common organic amendment.

quiz.q: Why should you stop irrigation 30 days before harvest?
quiz.explanation: Reducing water stress before harvest increases sugar concentration.
